title: Building Our Organizations For Today—and For What Comes Next
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez extends her earlier training-versus-enablement distinction by adding a third question: what the organization needs its people to become capable of over time. She explains that training works on a push model while enablement works on a pull model, embedding resources in the flow of daily work. Enablement helps people perform now, but long-term capability, such as managing people, using judgment with AI or navigating change, demands deeper, enterprise-level investment. Her argument is that lumping everything under L&D hides differences in what each approach requires and which problem it solves. She uses a house-building analogy from her tradesman father: you would not send an electrician to fix a foundation, so you need to know which part of the house you are working on. Naming the components properly leads to better decisions about tools, timing and sustained investment.
points: Training pushes curated learning to people, whereas enablement pulls support into the moment of work through job aids, searchable knowledge, AI tools and office hours.
Enablement makes today's work doable, but organizational capability looks ahead to what people must become able to do.
Real capability building needs practice, feedback, reinforcement, systems change and sustained investment, not surface-level interventions.
Calling all of this 'L&D' hides that training, enablement, knowledge management and performance support solve different problems.
Like a house build, you need to know which component you are working on before choosing the right tools and builders.
quotes: Unlike traditional training, which operates on more of a push model, wherein we decide what people need to learn, create a learning experience, and then push it to them in a highly curated environment, enablement operates on a pull model.

Enablement is incredibly powerful, but many organizations forget to resource for something else: What we need our people—and eventually our organization—to become increasingly capable of doing over time.

At the same time, sometimes we’re trying to develop something much deeper and more durable, and that will require more that surface-level interventions. It will require enterprise-level change in the form of practice, feedback, reinforcement, systems modification, culture reset, and sustained investment over time.
Enablement helps us make the work directly in front of people more doable, but capability asks us to look ahead and prepare ourselves for what we need to become.

Without seeing the parts of the whole broken down, we can’t make better decisions about how they fit together, where they belong, what they require, and what problem should be solved by who, when, and how.
In particular, we call an enormous collection of work L&D and then wonder why organizations struggle to build coherent learning infrastructure around it.
Once we know which part of the house we’re working on, we have a much better shot at bringing in the right tools, and building something that doesn’t just work well for today, but that lasts.
